payload.text: KnowledgeOps Sample Knowledge Base RAG Systems: Architecture, Retrieval, Evaluation and Reliability This sample document is designed for testing the KnowledgeOps RAG pipeline. It contains intentionally structured technical information that can be retrieved and cited by page number. 1. What is Retrieval-Augmented Generation? Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) combines information retrieval with a large language model. Instead of relying only on information encoded in model parameters, the system retrieves relevant external content and provides that content to the model as context before generating an answer. 2. RAG Architecture A typical RAG system contains a document ingestion pipeline and a query pipeline. The ingestion pipeline extracts text, splits documents into chunks, generates embeddings, and stores vectors with metadata. The query pipeline embeds the user question, retrieves candidate chunks, optionally reranks them, constructs context, and sends the context to an LLM. 3. Document Ingestion Document ingestion begins with validation. The system should check file type, file size, and whether meaningful text can be extracted. PDF documents can be processed page by page so that page metadata is preserved. Preserving document ID, filename, page number, and chunk ID makes later source citation possible. 4. Chunking Chunking divides a large document into smaller passages suitable for embedding and retrieval. A fixed character or token size can be used as a baseline, but chunk boundaries should ideally respect paragraphs, sections, tables, or other semantic boundaries. Chunk overlap can help preserve context between adjacent passages. 5. Embeddings An embedding model converts text into a numerical vector representing semantic information. Text passages with related meanings tend to have vectors that are closer together according to a chosen similarity measure. Both document chunks and user queries must be embedded using a compatible embedding model. 6. Vector Search The vector database stores embeddings together with their source metadata. During a query, the question embedding is compared with stored vectors and the highest-scoring candidates are returned. The number of candidates retrieved is commonly controlled with a Top-K parameter. 7. Reranking Vector search provides a candidate set, but the initial ranking may not always produce the best context for generation. A reranker can examine the query and candidate passages together and reorder them. A common pipeline is vector search for broad candidate retrieval followed by reranking to select a smaller high-quality context set. 8. Grounded Generation The generation stage receives the user's question and retrieved context. The system prompt should instruct the LLM to rely on the supplied evidence, avoid unsupported claims, and indicate when the retrieved information is insufficient. This reduces the risk of presenting unsupported statements as facts. 9. Source Citations A production RAG system should preserve source metadata throughout the pipeline. An answer can then cite the originating document and page. Source citations improve traceability because users can inspect the evidence used to construct an answer. 10. RAG Evaluation RAG evaluation should separately examine retrieval and generation. Retrieval evaluation can measure whether relevant passages were returned. Generation evaluation can examine answer relevance and whether claims are supported by the retrieved context. Citation correctness is another useful metric. 11. Observability Important RAG telemetry includes request ID, total latency, retrieval latency, reranking latency, LLM latency, number of retrieved chunks, retrieval scores, token usage, estimated cost, and errors. Structured logs should make it possible to trace a request across the pipeline. 12. Reliability AI systems depend on multiple external and internal components, so failures should be expected. Useful reliability mechanisms include request timeouts, bounded retries, exponential backoff, health checks, rate limiting, and graceful error responses. Permanent errors should not be retried indefinitely. 13. Example Production Flow A production-oriented flow can be summarized as: user question → validation → query embedding → vector retrieval → reranking → context construction → LLM generation → citation assembly → response. Each stage should have measurable latency and failure behavior.

EDIS: Enterprise Decision Intelligence System An AI-Powered Platform for Predictive Analytics, Risk Assessment, and Intelligent Project Governance Research Paper Title "EDIS: A Multi-Agent Retrieval-Augmented Decision Intelligence Framework for Predictive Enterprise Governance and Strategic Decision Support" 1. Introduction Modern enterprises generate vast amounts of structured and unstructured data through project documents, reports, emails, meeting notes, resource records, and operational systems. Despite this abundance of information, decision-makers often struggle to extract actionable insights quickly and accurately. Traditional project management and enterprise analytics tools primarily provide historical reporting rather than intelligent decision support. This results in delayed risk identification, inefficient resource allocation, project overruns, and reactive management practices. The proposed EDIS (Enterprise Decision Intelligence System) leverages Artificial Intelligence, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), Predictive Analytics, Multi-Agent Systems, and Explainable AI to create an intelligent enterprise decision-support ecosystem. 2. Abstract EDIS is an AI-powered Enterprise Decision Intelligence System designed to transform organizational decision-making through predictive insights, knowledge intelligence, and automated recommendations. The platform integrates enterprise document understanding, project risk prediction, resource optimization, intelligent reporting, and explainable decision support into a unified framework. By combining RAG-based knowledge retrieval, machine learning forecasting models, and autonomous AI agents, EDIS enables organizations to proactively identify risks, optimize operations, improve project outcomes, and support strategic planning through data-driven intelligence. 3. Problem Statement Organizations face several challenges in project and operational management: ● Critical information is distributed across multiple documents and systems. ● Project risks are often identified only after delays occur.
